title: Multiclass sample compression from binary compression
formal: Is the following implication valid for every function \(f:\mathbb N_0\to\mathbb N_0\)? Suppose every nonempty binary concept class \(B\subseteq\{0,1\}^{U}\) on every nonempty domain \(U\), with finite VC dimension \(v\), admits an exact realizable sample compression scheme of size at most \(f(v)\). Must there exist an integer \(A_f\ge1\) such that every nonempty multiclass concept class \(H\subseteq Y^X\), on arbitrary nonempty sets \(X,Y\) and with finite graph dimension \(d\), admits such a scheme of size at most \[A_f f(d)?\] The constant may depend on the chosen binary bound \(f\), but not on \(X,Y,H,d\), the sample size or the labels occurring in a sample. Label sets may be infinite. No properness, majority-vote form, stability, effectiveness or computational efficiency of the compression schemes is assumed. This restores the hypothesis omitted from the imported source sentence: the question concerns transfer of an arbitrary universal binary compression bound, not just existence of some graph-dimension bound.

source_formulation.text: If every binary class admits compression of size f of its VC dimension, must every multiclass class admit compression of size O(f of its graph dimension)?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

why: A general transfer theorem would carry any improvement in binary sample compression to multiclass prediction without a penalty for the number of labels. It would separate the combinatorial difficulty of binary compression from additional requirements imposed by multiclass reconstruction. This matters even though bounded compression at an exponential graph-dimension scale is already known.
status_note: Open Problem 5 in ALT 2025, retained as Open Problem 3.3 in the checked 7 April 2025 revision, asks for this general conditional transfer. The source proves it under additional reconstruction or stability assumptions and gives an extra label-count factor in the general finite-label case. Nearby impossibility results concern another dimension. No matching unrestricted transfer theorem or counterexample was found in the bounded search through 16 September 2026; this is not a proof of current openness.

category_assignment.reason: Sample compression and teaching in learning theory

importance.reason: A quantitative reduction connecting the central binary sample-compression problem to arbitrary-label multiclass prediction. It could transfer every improved universal binary bound without label-cardinality loss, while existing results require additional structure.

sentences: A compression scheme stores labeled examples and auxiliary bits so a fixed decoder can reproduce all labels of a realizable sample.
The question assumes a universal binary compression bound f in terms of VC dimension.
It asks whether every multiclass class then has compression of the same order in f of its graph dimension, independently of its label set.
Known reductions either pay an extra label-count factor or require additional structure of the binary scheme.
A complete Lean answer must establish the full conditional transfer or give an admissible binary bound for which that transfer fails.

definitions: \(\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). A concept is a function assigning a label to every instance. A finite labeled sample is a sequence \(S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n))\); repetitions and the empty sample are allowed. It is realizable by \(H\) if a single \(h\in H\) satisfies \(h(x_i)=y_i\) for every \(i\). A compression scheme for the fixed class is a pair of deterministic set functions \[\kappa:(X\times Y)^*\to(X\times Y)^*\times\{0,1\}^*,\qquad \rho:(X\times Y)^*\times\{0,1\}^*\to Y^X.\] Writing \(\kappa(S)=(S',b)\), every labeled record in \(S'\) must occur in \(S\). Following the source’s explicit convention that subset notation for sequences means inclusion of their underlying sets, the retained list may be reordered and may repeat a retained record. Every occurrence counts toward its length. No new or relabeled record may be introduced. The bit string \(b\) is auxiliary information. Size at most \(s\) means \(|S'|+|b|\le s\) on every finite input sample. The reconstruction receives only \(S',b\), not the original sample, its length, or the original positions of retained records. One retained labeled record costs one unit; one auxiliary bit costs one unit. Domain points and labels are mathematical objects, not charged by bit length. Exact realizable consistency means \(\rho(\kappa(S))(x_i)=y_i\) for every record of every realizable \(S\). The reconstructed function need not belong to \(H\), and no accuracy requirement is imposed on unrealizable samples. Both functions may depend on the complete class, but the same pair must work at all sample sizes. There is no randomness or failure probability. A binary class has VC dimension \(v\) when \(v\) is the largest size of a set of distinct domain points on which all binary label patterns occur. A multiclass class graph-shatters distinct points \(x_1,\ldots,x_r\) if there are reference labels \(a_1,\ldots,a_r\in Y\) such that every subset \(I\subseteq[r]\) has a hypothesis with \(h(x_i)=a_i\) exactly for \(i\in I\). The graph dimension is the largest such \(r\). Only classes of finite dimension enter the implication; dimension zero permits a size-zero scheme because all hypotheses agree pointwise. No monotonicity or computability assumption is placed on \(f\).
answer_criterion: Prove the universal implication in Lean, or prove its logical negation. A positive answer must show that every binary bound satisfying the premise transfers with a constant \(A_f\) uniform over all multiclass classes and all sample sizes; an effective black-box procedure is not required. A negative answer must exhibit one function \(f\) that really bounds compression for every binary class as stated, and prove that for every integer \(A\ge1\) some finite-graph-dimension multiclass class admits no compression scheme of size at most \(Af(d)\). Merely showing failure of a particular reduction does not refute the implication. A result with an extra label-count factor, an added structural requirement on the binary reconstruction, or a substituted dimension does not settle this question. The assertion concerns exact consistency and constant-factor size transfer; there is no numerical error tolerance.

context_blocks.text: Sample compression retains a few labeled examples and a few auxiliary bits, from which a fixed reconstruction rule must recover a predictor agreeing with the entire original realizable sample. It compresses the information needed for consistency, not the literal binary encoding of all discarded data. The size bound must hold regardless of the original sample length.

VC dimension records which binary patterns a class can realize on a finite set. Graph dimension asks which agreement and disagreement patterns with chosen reference labels a multiclass class can realize. These dimensions coincide for binary classes. The target uses graph dimension, not the different dimension characterizing general multiclass learnability.

Theorem 4 of the proceedings paper transfers any binary bound \(f(d)\) to a finite-label multiclass bound \(O(f(d)\log|Y|)\). The question asks whether that extra label-count cost can be removed without assumptions on the binary compression scheme. In the April 2025 revision the same open question is numbered 3.3.

The source removes the extra factor if the available binary reconstruction is proper or is a finite majority vote of class members; that result also covers infinite label sets. Proper means that the reconstructed binary predictor belongs to the class, and majority vote means pointwise voting among finitely many members, with ties assigned zero. The existence of an unrestricted binary compression scheme does not supply either property.

A separate result removes the extra factor for finite label spaces if the binary compressor is stable: removing records outside its retained set leaves its compressed message unchanged. The source treats infinite labels in that direction using a stronger extension of compression to infinite samples. Those are extra premises, so none is silently inserted into this card’s general finite-sample question.

Finite graph dimension already guarantees bounded compression of size \(2^{O(d)}\), and the source also gives size one for graph dimension one. These results do not establish transfer of every potentially smaller binary bound. In particular, proving a new binary bound would answer this card only if its multiclass consequence preserved the requested order.

Pabbaraju’s counterexample concerns multiclass learnability with a different dimension and an infinite label space. The paper explicitly distinguishes finite graph dimension, where bounded compression is available. Thus the broad slogan that multiclass learnability does not imply compression does not refute this finite-graph-dimension reduction.
